title: Buffering
body:
Holding data in an intermediate store so the producer and the consumer do not have to be
in step. An [[I-O Device]] needs it for three reasons, and they are the three worth
remembering:

- **Speed differences.** A keyboard produces a few bytes a second, a [[CPU]] executes
  millions of instructions in the same time. Without a buffer the fast side waits on the
  slow one, or the slow side loses data.
- **Data format differences.** The device may work in bits ([[Serial I-O]]), the CPU in
  words. A [[Shift Register]] buffering a byte is what bridges that.
- **Electronic differences.** Voltage levels, drive strength, and timing on the device
  side are not the bus's.

Miss the window on an unbuffered read and you get an [[overrun]]: the next byte arrives
before you took the last one.

**Double buffering** is the two-buffer version, one being filled while the other is
drained; the graphics case is [[Double Buffering]].

This concept comes back in [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] as kernel I/O buffering and the
producer-consumer problem, where the buffer is a shared circular [[Queue]] and the
interesting part becomes [[Synchronization]] rather than electronics.
